transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-08-01 16:00 PDT | Duration: 42m | Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ethan Ruiz (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (Tidewater CTO), Priya Singh (Lead ML Eng), Aaron Vega (Platform Eng)

Summary: Quick POC weekly sync to review cost/unit economics, caching savings observed in last run, discuss batching tradeoffs and define next steps for a 24h steady-state benchmark. Some audio dropouts, occasional mis-transcriptions (KV cache sometimes as 'K V cash').

Topics: results review, tokens/sec/$, cache hit-rates, latency SLOs, dedicated vs hosted routing, next steps / benchmarks.

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, welcome. should we do a very quick run of notes — main objective is to align on cost per unit and next benchmark.
[00:22] Liam: Yeah thanks. we've seen the dashboard, and the big question from our side is, what are realistic tokens per dollar numbers if we turn on prefix caching + smaller batch sizes to keep p90 under 300ms.
[00:38] Ethan: cool, i can start with the numbers we observed. last 48h run (mix A, see sheet link) we measured about 1,700 tokens/sec/$ for plain baseline on g5-like hardware with no caching. With prefix/KV cache enabled we saw effective improvement to ~3,200 tokens/sec/$ for the same model variant — that's aggregated when cache hit-rate is >40%.
[01:05] Priya: wait can you repeat the cache hit percent? i thought our runs were closer to 25%.
[01:12] Ethan: right — that 3,200 number was from the warm window where hit-rate hit 45%. the average across the 48h was ~32% which yields ~2,400 tokens/sec/$. the improvement is nonlinear — most savings come from long shared prefixes in our request shape.
[01:34] Aaron: and what's the latency impact when cache hits? we need to keep p95 below 400ms ideally.
[01:40] Ethan: cache hits are faster — median goes down by ~70ms, p95 improves a bit but you still have RPC overhead for some retrievals, so p95 stays around 320-380ms depending on batching.
[02:02] Maya: important context — your production mix matters. our suggestion is to profile with the exact prompt set you expect at 75% traffic. we'll run a 24h steady-state to get realistic numbers.
[02:15] Liam: okay, walk me through batching tradeoffs. we saw a spike in tokens/sec/$ when we increased batch_size to 32 but latency p95 jumped above 600ms.
[02:28] Ethan: yep that's classic. larger batches improve throughput and amortize kernel startup, so tokens per dollar looks great. but tail latency becomes worse because requests wait to fill the batch. We recommend adaptive batching: use a small max latency cap (e.g., 120ms wait) so short queries don't block. For Tidewater's mix (short logistics prompts + occasional long summaries) a mixed policy helps.
[02:58] Priya: can Redwood enforce an adaptive policy? like batch size cap + max wait?
[03:05] Maya: yes, our runtime supports wait-time and max batch size knobs, plus priority routing by route. Ethan can show a config snippet after.
[03:15] Ethan: (share link) here's the config we used: max_batch: 16, max_wait_ms: 120, prefer_small_requests: true. We'll try another sweep with max_batch 8 and 16 to show delta.
[03:34] Liam: what about dedicated capacity vs hosted — we want predictability.
[03:38] Maya: Dedicated gives stable throughput and you can pin GPUs; hosted is more elastic and cheaper for bursty traffic. For tight SLOs and steady high qps, Dedicated reserved pools are usually recommended. But caching and batching reduce effective capacity needs, so we can show both scenarios in cost sheet.
[03:58] Aaron: security question — with prefix caching are any tokens persisted in Redwood logs or are they ecrypted at rest?
[04:06] Maya: logs are obfuscated by default; cache entries are encrypted at rest and access-controlled. we'll send the security whitepaper. also if you need on-prem or VPC mode that's an option for full data residency.
[04:20] Priya: great, please include cache TTL options; sometimes we want only 30 minutes for ephemeral content.
[04:26] Ethan: TTL configurable per route — we can set short TTLs (e.g., 10-30m) for sensitive prompts. note that shorter TTL reduces cache hit-rate and thus tokens/$ benefits.
[04:40] [07:00] (audio drop)
[07:05] Liam: back — about the tokens/sec/$ numbers, can you break down compute vs infra network costs?
[07:12] Ethan: sure. most of the saving from caching is compute — fewer forward passes. network is small but not zero because KV retrievals add RPC costs. In the spreadsheet i posted, we broke out GPU-hr equivalent and network egress per 1M tokens. I'll re-share with line items.
[07:35] Priya: i saw one run where batching gave 2.8x tokens/sec/$ improvement but latency was awful. Are there hybrid approaches?
[07:44] Ethan: yes — we do latency-sensitive lanes with small batch caps and a bulk lane for batch-optimized requests. The runtime can route by route header or by a lightweight classification. That way customer-facing UI requests stay fast while back-office summarization uses larger batches.
[08:05] Aaron: can we tag traffic so we can measure cost per logical-op? We want per-feature costing.
[08:11] Maya: absolutely, you can send route metadata and we'll produce per-route cost breakdowns in Console.
[08:18] Liam: ok next question — degradation/fallback. If the dedicated pool is saturated, can Redwood fallback to a cheaper model variant automatically?
[08:26] Ethan: yes, we support model-variant fallbacks and region fallback. You can specify quality thresholds and fallback chains. We'll propose a two-tier fallback: primary high-quality model for 90% of requests, and a quantized variant for bulk loads. We'll include quality regression numbers in the sheet.
[08:48] Priya: any example numbers for quantized model accuracy drop?
[08:52] Ethan: for your summarization task we saw a BLEU-like proxy drop ~2-4% on 4-bit quant vs fp16. often acceptable for non-critical paths. We'll attach eval results.
[09:03] Liam: sounds good. please call out which routes are safe for fallback.
[09:08] Maya: we'll annotate that in the spreadsheet and show cost tradeoffs per route.
[09:12] [12:10] Priya: question on the billing model — tokens/sec/$ is useful but we need predicted monthly cost at 5M requests per month.
[12:20] Ethan: the sheet contains a per-1M token line and a scenario calc. Quick offhand: with caching hit-rate at 35% and adaptive batching we estimate $7.8k/month for your 5M request estimate (assumes avg tokens/request ~450). If hit-rate is 20% cost jumps to ~12k. We'll run the 24h run with your sample set to firm numbers.
[12:46] Aaron: can we get a CSV export of per-route token counts + cost?
[12:49] Maya: yes, we'll export per-route usage and predicted spend.
[13:00] Liam: Priya — what's your internal timeline for ramp?
[13:04] Priya: we want a small pilot in two weeks, and then ramp to prod in 8 weeks if numbers look good. security ok and SLOs met.
[13:14] Maya: good, that fits our recommended cadence. we'll prioritize the steady-state benchmark this week.
[13:20] Ethan: follow-up on numbers to run: we'll do a 24h at 75% production mix, plus two sweeps for batching (max_batch 8 and 16) and cache TTL at 30m and 2h.
[13:37] Priya: please include request sampling for edge cases; we saw one input that forces long context windows.
[13:43] Ethan: good call — we'll include the long-context bucket and show tokens/second for those.
[13:48] [20:00] (murmur, background)
[20:35] Liam: procurement quirk — are there minimum commitments if we go Dedicated?
[20:40] Maya: Dedicated typically has a monthly commit for reserved capacity; we'll share a few pricing bands. For pilot we recommend hosted and then evaluate Dedicated once we have stable demand.
[20:52] Aaron: what about SSO and audit logs for compliance?
[20:56] Maya: SSO via SAML, SCIM for provisioning, and full audit logs available for enterprise plans. We'll include SOC2 attestation link.
[21:10] Priya: anything else on tuning? specifically on cache warm-up in morning peak?
[21:15] Ethan: warm-up matters. If your traffic is diurnal, cache warming ahead of peak yields disproportionate wins. We'll show warm-up scripts for the pilot so morning hit-rate isn't zero.
[21:30] Liam: can Redwood run a warm-up wave as part of the benchmark?
[21:33] Maya: yes we can schedule a warm-up pass before the 24h measurement window.
[21:37] Ethan: also note long tail tokens from rarely-seen prompts won't benefit — that's expected. focus on high-frequency prefixes.
[22:00] [30:00] recap pause
[30:05] Maya: quick recap of this call: 1) Redwood will run 24h steady-state benchmark (75% mix) + batching sweeps and TTL sweeps; 2) we will produce a CSV with per-route cost and tokens and a recommended config; 3) Priya will share traces and peak SLOs; 4) Maya will send security docs and cost sheet.
[30:32] Priya: confirmed. also date for next sync? we'd like quick results early next week.
[30:37] Maya: we'll aim to have benchmark and sheet by Mon 2026-08-03. next sync Thurs if needed.
[30:45] Aaron: one more — can Redwood simulate a 2x traffic spike to test autoscaling behavior?
[30:50] Ethan: yes, we'll include a burst test during the run. we'll show throttling and fallback behavior.
[31:00] Liam: great. thanks everyone.
[31:05] [41:58] (meeting ends)
